original_question: For N = {1,2,...,n}, determine the largest subset of N with the property that no m elements of the subset form an arithmetic progression, and ask the analogous question when geometric progressions are forbidden instead. More generally, for a given m-ary relation R on a set N, determine the largest subset whose m-element subsets never satisfy R, including the case where N is infinite such as an interval of real numbers.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 24 (tagged "On van der Waerden's theorem")
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the full three-part structure of Unsolved Problem 24: first, the extremal problem for N = {1,2,...,n} with no m-term arithmetic progression; second, the analogous question for geometric progressions; and third, the paper's broader reformulation for a general m-ary relation R, including the extension to an infinite ambient set exemplified by an interval of R (Unsolved Problem 24, P20-P21).
missing_details: The paper explicitly assumes integers n and m with n > m > 2.
The finite ambient set is exactly N = {1,2,...,n}.
The optimization is over subsets A of N and asks for the maximum cardinality of such a subset.
The phrase "any m from these" should be made stand-alone as: every choice of m distinct elements of A fails to form the prohibited progression/relation.
The paper states the generalization as: "Let R be a given m-ary relation on a field N," so that literal wording should be noted if one wants maximal fidelity to the source.
The infinite-set extension is not just "N infinite" in general; the paper specifically asks what happens when the ambient set has "continuation power," with an interval of R given as the example.
The paper explicitly frames the problem as being in the context of van der Waerden's theorem.
refined_question: For fixed integers n and m with n > m > 2, let N = {1,2,...,n}. Determine the maximum cardinality of a subset A ⊆ N such that no m distinct elements of A form an arithmetic progression. Ask the analogous extremal question when "arithmetic progression" is replaced by "geometric progression." More generally, given an ambient set X (the paper literally says "a field N") together with an m-ary relation R, determine the largest possible cardinality of a subset A ⊆ X such that no m distinct elements of A satisfy R; in particular, what is the corresponding extremal problem when X has continuum size, for example when X is an interval of R?
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Unsolved Problem 24, whose wording matches your draft almost line for line: it starts with N = {1,2,...,n}, asks for the maximum number of extracted elements avoiding m-term arithmetic progressions, then asks the same for geometric progressions, and finally generalizes to a given m-ary relation R and asks about the continuum-size case "for example when N is an interval from R" (Unsolved Problem 24, P20-P21). Although the paper later has a nearby problem about infinite sequences avoiding arithmetic/geometric progressions, that is Unsolved Problem 28 and it asks instead about the reciprocal sum Σ 1/a_n and related bijectivity questions, so your draft is targeting Problem 24 rather than that neighboring problem (Unsolved Problem 28, P23-P24). The abstract also confirms that arithmetic and geometric progressions are among the paper's central themes (Abstract, P0).
